summary_html: CPS **accepts** a report for **investigation/assessment**. CAPTA sets the floor for investigation procedures; CFSR evaluates timeliness, safety, and decision quality.
authority_html:
- **CAPTA (42 U.S.C. §§ 5101–5116)** — investigation standards tied to funding  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — timeliness & response conformity indicators

primary_citations.citation_text: Texas - Texas Family Code Chapter 261 (Investigation of Report of Child Abuse or Neglect)
Texas - Texas Family Code Chapter 262 (Procedures in Suit by Governmental Entity to Protect Health and Safety of Child)

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: Gates v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The government may not seize a child from his parents absent a court order, parental consent or exigent circumstances, exigency meaning reasonable cause to believe the child is in imminent danger of physical or sexual abuse; an uncorroborated anonymous tip will rarely suffice. Because that law was not clearly established when these events occurred, every individual defendant received qualified immunity and summary judgment was affirmed.
key_cases.relevance: Once intake accepts a report, Gates governs what the investigation may actually do — entry into the home requires consent, exigency or a court order, and interviewing the children on the premises is a search and seizure question, not a matter of agency discretion.
key_cases.quote: an anonymous tip regarding child abuse will rarely be sufficient to justify the seizure of a child

key_cases.case_name: Roe v. Texas Department of Protective & Regulatory Services
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: A CPS caseworker's visual body-cavity search of a child raised a Fourth Amendment claim, and in non-exigent circumstances the worker must obtain a warrant or court order rather than proceed on a parent's silence; a parent's consent to an investigative home interview is not consent to such a search, and consent to entry may be revoked. Because those rights were not clearly established, the worker received qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: Marks the line between an accepted report and what the accepted report permits — consent to an investigative home visit does not carry consent to search the child's body.
key_cases.quote: In non-exigent circumstances, the worker then has time to obtain a warrant either personally to conduct a visual body cavity search or to have a physician perform it.

search_keywords: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

state_agency.name: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services

notice_requirements.timing: In writing before the department conducts an interview with an alleged perpetrator; the person signs the written notice to acknowledge receipt (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))
content_required: That the person may request an administrative review of the department's findings under Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309 (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(a))

Administrative review of a disputed determination of whether child abuse or neglect occurred is conducted by a department employee in administration who was not involved in and did not directly supervise the investigation, and the review must sustain, alter, or reverse the department's original findings (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(c))

The review must be conducted as soon as possible but not later than the 45th day after the date the department receives the request, unless the department has good cause for extending the deadline or a related court proceeding or criminal investigation is pending (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(d))
notice_requirements.defective_notice_consequence: Not specified in Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091; the department must document in the case file that it provided the notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.3091(b)). A person is not required to exhaust the review remedy before pursuing a judicial remedy provided by law (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.309(e)), and when a finding is overturned the department must remove the person's name from the central registry not later than the 10th business day after it receives notice (Tex. Fam. Code § 261.002(b)(3))
